definition: Measuring how well an AI model performs on the tasks it is meant to do, including quality, safety and reliability.
details: Evaluation uses benchmarks, held-out datasets and human judgment to score accuracy, robustness, fairness and other properties. For language models, holistic suites such as HELM run many benchmarks together because no single metric captures real-world usefulness.

explainer.lead: Evaluation measures whether a model actually does its intended job on quality, safety and reliability, not just whether it trains. It is the main evidence behind any claim that one model is better than another.

tiers.eli5: It is like test-driving a car on many roads instead of just checking the engine starts: you find out how it actually behaves where it matters.
tiers.practitioner: Teams combine held-out datasets, benchmarks and human judgment, and often run holistic suites because no single metric captures usefulness. A pitfall is overfitting to benchmarks or letting evaluation data leak into training, which inflates scores without improving real performance.
tiers.paperLevel: Evaluation scores a model on task-specific metrics (accuracy, robustness, fairness) over held-out data; aggregate suites such as HELM run many benchmarks together because real-world usefulness is multi-dimensional. Known limits: benchmarks saturate and drift from real use, and human judgment is costly and noisy.

explainer.example: A team scores a new chat model on accuracy, safety-refusal rates and human preference over a held-out prompt set, reporting all three rather than a single number.
